analogy.p: Think of a parabola as the profile of a valley (a > 0) or a hill (a < 0). The turning point is the lowest point of the valley floor or the top of the hill, and the line of symmetry is the vertical line running through it, like a fold in a piece of paper. Completing the square is like the surveyor's description of that landmark: 'start at the origin, go p to the side and q up or down'. The roots are where the valley's walls cross sea level (the x-axis); if the valley floor is above sea level, the stream never reaches the sea, which matches having no real roots. The analogy breaks down because a real valley is not a perfect parabola and a graph carries on forever in both directions.

bullets: **Roots** (x-intercepts, zeros, solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0) are the x-values where y = 0, i.e. where the graph meets the x-axis.
The **y-intercept** is where x = 0, so it is simply the constant term **c**.
The **turning point** is the lowest point (minimum, if a > 0) or highest point (maximum, if a < 0).
The **line of symmetry** is a vertical line x = k through the turning point; each side of the parabola is a mirror image of the other.
A quadratic can have **two roots**, **one repeated root** (the curve just touches the x-axis at its turning point) or **no real roots** (the curve never reaches the x-axis).
The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is always a smooth curve: never straight segments, never a pointed or flat bottom.
Higher tier skill: given the graph, **read** these features; given the equation, **work them out algebraically**; and link both.
core.h: The quadratic graph and its key features
core.p: A **quadratic function** has the form y = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Its graph is a smooth symmetrical curve called a **parabola**. If **a is positive** the curve is U-shaped (a minimum turning point); if **a is negative** it is ∩-shaped (a maximum turning point). The Edexcel specification asks you to **identify and interpret roots, intercepts and turning points of quadratic functions graphically**, and to **deduce the turning point by completing the square**. Four features describe any parabola: where it crosses the x-axis (the **roots**), where it crosses the y-axis (the **y-intercept**), its **turning point**, and its **line of symmetry**.

bullets: For y = x² − 4x + 3 the roots satisfy x² − 4x + 3 = 0, (x − 1)(x − 3) = 0, so **x = 1 and x = 3**; the y-intercept is **(0, 3)**.
A graph that **touches** the x-axis without crossing has a **repeated root**: y = (x − 2)² touches at x = 2, and its turning point is on the x-axis.
A graph that stays **completely above** (or below) the x-axis has **no real roots**; this means the quadratic never equals 0.
In completed-square form y = (x + p)² + q: there are real roots only if (x + p)² = −q has a solution, i.e. when **q ≤ 0** for an upright parabola.
The solutions of x² + 6x + 2 = 0 are irrational, so factorising fails; completing the square gives exact answers in surd form.
In a context question, **always write the answer with units** and decide whether a root makes sense (a negative time may be rejected).
If asked to 'solve' using a graph, give answers to the accuracy the grid allows (usually 1 decimal place) and show where you read them.
core.h: Roots and intercepts from a graph and from algebra
core.p: To find the roots **graphically** you read the x-coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis. To find them **algebraically** you set y = 0 and solve ax² + bx + c = 0 by **factorising**, by the **quadratic formula** or by **completing the square**. The y-intercept needs no solving: put x = 0 and you get y = c. When a question asks you to 'interpret' roots, remember they are the points where the output is zero, which in context might be the time when a ball hits the ground, or a break-even point.

bullets: x-coordinate of the turning point = (sum of the roots) ÷ 2.
For y = ax² + bx + c, the line of symmetry is **x = −b/(2a)** (a useful check; you do not need to prove it at GCSE).
Check: y = 2x² + 12x + 5 has line of symmetry x = −12/4 = −3; y = 3x² − 12x + 7 has x = 12/6 = 2.
After finding the x-coordinate, **substitute it into the equation** to get the y-coordinate of the turning point.
Symmetry also gives you extra points: if (0, 3) is on the graph and the line of symmetry is x = 2 then (4, 3) is also on the graph.
**Minimum value** of the function = y-coordinate of a minimum turning point (and the **x-value** at which it occurs is its x-coordinate).
The range of an upright parabola is **y ≥ minimum value**; of an ∩-shaped parabola, y ≤ maximum value.
The turning point is also called the **vertex**.
core.p: The turning point is on the line of symmetry, so its x-coordinate is **exactly halfway between the two roots** when the roots exist. In the example y = x² − 4x + 3 the roots are 1 and 3, the midpoint is 2, so the turning point is at x = 2, and y = 2² − 4(2) + 3 = −1, giving **(2, −1)**. The symmetry also explains why the two ends of the curve are at the same height for equal distances from the line. This 'midpoint of the roots' trick is quick, but it only works when you know the roots, whereas **completing the square works every time**, even when there are no real roots.

bullets: **Step 1:** halve the coefficient of x. For x² + 6x + 2 half of 6 is **3**.
**Step 2:** write the bracket (x + 3)² with the same sign as the x-term.
**Step 3:** subtract the square of the half: **− 3² = − 9**.
**Step 4:** add the original constant: **+ 2**. So x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = **(x + 3)² − 7**.
**Check by expanding:** (x + 3)² − 7 = x² + 6x + 9 − 7 = x² + 6x + 2. ✓ Always do this check.
**Negative b:** x² − 8x + 3 = (x − 4)² − 16 + 3 = **(x − 4)² − 13**; the bracket takes the sign of the x-term.
In exam language: 'write in the form (x + a)² + b' means give both **a** and **b** as numbers, which can be negative.
core.p: Completing the square rewrites **x² + bx + c** in the form **(x + p)² + q**. The idea is that (x + p)² expands to x² + 2px + p², so to match the x-term, **p must be half of b**. Expanding (x + p)² gives an extra p² which is not in the original expression, so you **subtract p²** to compensate, and keep the constant c. The result is **x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c**. The area picture on the right makes the reason visible: x² + 6x is a square plus two strips, and adding the missing 3 × 3 corner completes a square of side (x + 3).

bullets: y = (x + 3)² − 7: turning point **(−3, −7)**, symmetry x = −3 (see the translation figure).
y = (x − 4)² − 13: turning point **(4, −13)**.
y = (x + 5)² + 2: turning point (−5, 2); because q is positive and above the x-axis, there are **no real roots**.
y = (x − 2)² − 1: turning point (2, −1) (the graph on the left).
**Minimum value** of x² − 8x + 3 is −13, occurring at x = 4.
The y-intercept comes from putting x = 0 in either form: (0 − 4)² − 13 = 3. ✓
Link to graph transformations: y = (x + p)² + q is y = x² translated by the vector **(−p, q)**.
Common mistake: giving the turning point as (p, q) instead of (−p, q).
core.h: Reading the turning point from (x + p)² + q
core.p: The completed square form is a **translation of y = x²**. Since (x + p)² is never negative and is 0 only when x = −p, the smallest possible value of y is q, and it happens at x = −p. Therefore **the turning point of y = (x + p)² + q is (−p, q)**, a minimum for an upright parabola. Notice the sign flip: the number in the bracket gives the x-coordinate with the **opposite sign**, while the number outside gives the y-coordinate **as written**. The line of symmetry is **x = −p**.

bullets: Method: **factor a out of the first two terms**: 3x² − 12x + 7 = 3(x² − 4x) + 7.
Complete the square inside: x² − 4x = (x − 2)² − 4, so 3[(x − 2)² − 4] + 7.
**Multiply the −4 by 3:** 3(x − 2)² − 12 + 7 = **3(x − 2)² − 5**. Turning point (2, −5); minimum value −5.
Check by expanding: 3(x − 2)² − 5 = 3x² − 12x + 12 − 5 = 3x² − 12x + 7. ✓
For 2x² + 12x + 5 = 2(x + 3)² − 13: turning point (−3, −13) and y-intercept 2(9) − 13 = 5. ✓
If the question gives the form **a(x + p)² + q** you must identify all three numbers a, p and q.
Alternatively divide every term by a (when it divides exactly) to make a = 1, solve, then restore.
Do **not** put a inside the constant: 2(x + 3)² − 9 + 5 is wrong because the −9 is multiplied by 2.
core.p: When the coefficient of x² is not 1, first **factor out a from the x² and x terms only** (leave the constant outside), complete the square on what is inside the bracket, then **multiply out the extra term by a** to bring it back outside. For 2x² + 12x + 5: write 2(x² + 6x) + 5 = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] + 5 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 5 = **2(x + 3)² − 13**. The general form is **a(x + p)² + q** and the turning point is still **(−p, q)**. The extra step of multiplying the −9 by 2 is where marks are most often lost.

bullets: Take care with signs: −[(x − 2)² − 4] = −(x − 2)² + 4 (the **−4 becomes +4**).
The curve is ∩-shaped; the maximum value is the number outside; the range is y ≤ maximum.
This form is used for **maximum height** and **maximum profit** problems.
To find roots from −(x − 2)² + 5 = 0 rearrange to (x − 2)² = 5, so x = 2 ± √5.
Sketch: ∩-shaped curve, roots at 2 ± √5 (about −0.24 and 4.24), y-intercept (0, 1) and maximum (2, 5) (see figure).
core.h: Completing the square with a negative x² coefficient (maximum points)
core.p: When the x² term is negative, factor out the **negative** number: −x² + 4x + 1 = −(x² − 4x) + 1 = −[(x − 2)² − 4] + 1 = −(x − 2)² + 4 + 1 = **−(x − 2)² + 5**. Because −(x − 2)² is never positive, its biggest value is 0 and the whole expression has a **maximum value of 5 when x = 2**. The turning point is therefore **(2, 5)**, a maximum. This is the reflection of an upright parabola in the x-axis, which links directly to graph transformations.

bullets: Half of b = half of 5 is **2.5**, half of −7 is **−3.5**.
Square the fraction carefully: (3/2)² = 9/4 = 2.25; (5/2)² = 25/4 = 6.25.
Leave surds exact if the question says 'give your answer in surd form'.
If the question says 'give your answer to 3 significant figures' round only at the end.
Use your calculator for the final decimal but show the exact form first for the method mark.
core.p: If the coefficient of x is odd, half of it is a fraction or decimal. Do not worry: use the same method. For x² + 3x + 1, half of 3 is 1.5 (or 3/2), so x² + 3x + 1 = (x + 3/2)² − 9/4 + 1 = **(x + 3/2)² − 5/4**. Fractions are usually preferred to decimals when the answer is exact, though (x + 1.5)² − 1.25 is also acceptable. The turning point is then **(−1.5, −1.25)**. Check by expanding: (x + 1.5)² − 1.25 = x² + 3x + 2.25 − 1.25 = x² + 3x + 1. ✓

bullets: **Step 1:** write in completed-square form. **Step 2:** rearrange to (x + p)² = k. **Step 3:** take ±√k. **Step 4:** subtract p.
The ± matters: forgetting the negative square root loses an accuracy mark and a root.
If k is negative (e.g. (x − 3)² = −1) there are **no real solutions**.
If k = 0 there is **one repeated root**.
For 'solve by completing the square' marks: M1 for the completed square, M1 for rearranging, A1 for each root.
Compare with the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a, which comes from completing the square on ax² + bx + c = 0 in general.
core.h: Solving quadratic equations by completing the square
core.p: Completing the square is the method that always works. To solve x² + 6x + 2 = 0: complete the square to get (x + 3)² − 7 = 0, **add 7** to both sides: (x + 3)² = 7, **square root both sides** (remembering the plus and minus): x + 3 = ±√7, and finally **subtract 3**: x = −3 ± √7. This gives the exact answers −3 + √7 ≈ −0.354 and −3 − √7 ≈ −5.646. The quadratic formula is exactly this procedure done once for general a, b, c, which is why it always gives the same answers.

bullets: Model: 'x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1. Since (x − 3)² ≥ 0 for all x, the expression is ≥ 1, so it is always positive.'
Least value = the number outside the bracket, occurring when the bracket is zero (here x = 3).
To show an expression is **always negative** use −(x − p)² − k with k > 0.
Show that x² + 4x + 7 > 0: (x + 2)² + 3 ≥ 3 > 0.
A curve with a minimum turning point **above** the x-axis does not intersect it, so the equation has no real solutions.
Link with the discriminant: b² − 4ac < 0 means no real roots; for x² − 6x + 10, 36 − 40 = −4 < 0.
Always write the **inequality symbol** correctly: ≥ for the bracket, > for the final statement.
core.h: Proving a quadratic is always positive (or finding least/greatest values)
core.p: Completing the square is the standard way to **show that an expression is always positive or always negative**, or to find its **least or greatest value**. A squared bracket is never negative, so (x − 3)² ≥ 0 for every x. For x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1, the smallest value of the bracket is 0, so the smallest value of the expression is 1, which means it is **always greater than 0** and has **no real roots**. A full-mark answer states both the completed square and the reason in words.

bullets: Turning point (3, −2) and a = 1: y = (x − 3)² − 2 = x² − 6x + 7.
Check: expand (x − 3)² − 2 = x² − 6x + 9 − 2. ✓
Compare coefficients: **b = 2p** and **c = p² + q**.
If a point on the curve is given, substitute it into y = a(x − h)² + k to find a.
Example: turning point (1, 4) and passes through (0, 2): 2 = a(0 − 1)² + 4, so a = −2, y = −2(x − 1)² + 4.
The identity symbol ≡ means 'true for all values of x', which is why you can compare coefficients.
Use the line of symmetry x = h to find other points, e.g. the other root.
core.h: Finding the equation from the turning point
core.p: If you are told a quadratic has turning point (h, k) and a = 1, its equation is **y = (x − h)² + k**. Expand it if the question wants the form x² + bx + c. You can also reverse the process: given x² + bx + c ≡ (x + p)² + q, **compare coefficients**: b = 2p and c = p² + q. For x² − 8x + 11 ≡ (x + p)² + q this gives 2p = −8, so p = −4, and 11 = 16 + q, so q = −5. The turning point is (4, −5).

bullets: When it lands h = 0: (t − 2)² = 4.2, t = 2 + √4.2 = **4.05 s** (reject the negative root as time cannot be negative).
The y-intercept h = 1 is the height at the start (t = 0).
Always give **units** and answer in the context of the question.
A maximum profit question works the same: the turning point (price, profit) gives the best price.
If the graph has no real roots, the ball never reaches the ground in the model, which is a clue the model is wrong.
The symmetry says the ball is at the same height at t = 1 and t = 3 (equal distances either side of 2).
core.p: Many real situations have quadratic graphs: the height of a ball against time, area against length, profit against price. The **turning point** gives the **maximum or minimum** of the situation (greatest height, least cost), and the **roots** give when the quantity is zero (when the ball hits the ground). Completing the square gives these directly. For a ball with height h = −5t² + 20t + 1 (metres, t in seconds): h = −5(t − 2)² + 21, so the maximum height is **21 m** after **2 seconds**.

bullets: **Factorising** x² + bx + c finds roots directly if they are integers; completing the square always works.
**Quadratic formula:** derived by completing the square on ax² + bx + c.
**Graph transformations:** (x + p)² + q is y = x² translated by (−p, q); −f(x) reflects in the x-axis.
**Surds:** answers like −3 ± √7 must be simplified (e.g. √12 = 2√3).
**Inequalities:** the range is y ≥ q or y ≤ q.
**Proof:** showing an expression is always positive uses a perfect square being ≥ 0.
**Differentiation (A-level):** the turning point is where the gradient is zero; completing the square is a pre-calculus way to find it.
**Sketching:** for the full sketch give roots, y-intercept, turning point and a smooth parabola.
core.p: Turning points and completing the square draw on **expanding and factorising**, **solving equations**, **graph transformations**, **surds**, **inequalities** (ranges) and **proof**. They are examined on both calculator and non-calculator papers, often as multi-step questions: complete the square, state the turning point, then sketch or solve. Learn the sequence so you can score every mark.

exam: **Typical marks:** write in the form (x + a)² + b = 2 marks; hence state the turning point = 1 mark; solve by completing the square = 3 to 4 marks; show an expression is always positive = 2 to 3 marks.

**Command words:** 'Write in the form (x + p)² + q' needs the completed square; 'Hence' means you must use your previous answer; 'Show that' needs a fully written proof; 'Sketch' needs shape, intercepts and turning point labelled.
**Always check by expanding** the completed square back to the original: it takes 10 seconds and catches the commonest slips.
For turning point questions write: 'Turning point (−p, q)' with brackets and a comma; if asked for the **minimum value** give only the number q.

In **solving** questions, write the exact answer first (−3 ± √7), then the rounded value to the accuracy requested (e.g. −0.354 and −5.65 to 3 s.f.). If it says 'give answers in surd form' do not round.
For 'show that' always-positive questions, write: completed square, the statement '(x − 3)² ≥ 0', then the conclusion '(expression) ≥ 1 > 0'.
On a sketch of a quadratic, label the **y-intercept, roots (if any) and the turning point**; draw a smooth parabola the right way up (U for positive a, ∩ for negative a).
For 4 and 6 mark problem-solving questions (e.g. maximum height or area), set up the quadratic, complete the square, then interpret the answer **in context with units**.
Calculator papers allow you to check roots with the equation solver, but you still need the algebra for the method marks.
If the question gives the form a(x + p)² + q, equate expansions or follow the factor-first method; state the values of a, p and q clearly.

mistakes.r: Halve the coefficient: (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7. Always check by expanding.
Expanding (x + 3)² gives an extra 9, so you must subtract 9: (x + 3)² − 7.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to subtract the square: x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² + 2.

mistakes.r: The turning point is (−3, −7): the sign of the number in the bracket is reversed for the x-coordinate.
It is (4, 2); the x-coordinate is the number that makes the bracket zero.
Factor a out of the x² and x terms only; leave the constant outside the bracket.
mistakes.w: Factorising out a from all three terms, including the constant.

mistakes.r: Take both square roots: x = −3 ± √7, giving two solutions.
With a negative coefficient of x² the curve is ∩-shaped, so (2, 5) is a maximum.
mistakes.w: Calling the turning point of y = −(x − 2)² + 5 a minimum.

mistakes.r: A parabola is a smooth rounded curve, symmetrical about the vertical line through the turning point.
mistakes.w: Drawing a parabola with a pointed or flat turning point, or straight-line segments.

summary: Edexcel Higher asks you to identify and interpret the roots, intercepts and turning point of a quadratic from its graph, and to use completing the square to deduce the turning point and solve quadratic equations. It matters because it is a frequent multi-mark question on all three papers and links algebra, graphs and proof.

Completing the square with areas: x² + 6x is a square and two strips; adding the missing 3 × 3 corner completes a square of side (x + 3), so you must subtract 9 to balance.

terms.d: A function of the form y = ax² + bx + c, where a ≠ 0.
The smooth symmetrical U-shaped or ∩-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic function.
A value of x for which the function equals zero; where the graph crosses the x-axis.
A point where the graph crosses an axis; the y-intercept of a quadratic is (0, c).
The point where a curve changes direction: the minimum or maximum point of a parabola.
The lowest turning point of a graph; for y = ax² + bx + c this occurs when a > 0.
The highest turning point of a graph; for a parabola this occurs when a < 0.
The vertical line through the turning point that divides the parabola into two mirror halves, x = −p for y = (x + p)² + q.
Rewriting x² + bx + c in the form (x + p)² + q.
A root that occurs twice, when the graph touches (but does not cross) the x-axis at its turning point.
Roots that are real numbers, i.e. where the graph meets the x-axis.
An irrational root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction, such as √7; exact answers are left in surd form.
The number multiplying a variable (in 6x the coefficient of x is 6).
An equation that is true for every value of the variable, such as x² + 6x + 2 ≡ (x + 3)² − 7.
Another name for the turning point of a parabola.
The expression b² − 4ac; negative means no real roots, zero means a repeated root, positive means two real roots.

worked.q: (a) Write x² + 8x + 3 in the form (x + a)² + b. (b) Write down the coordinates of the turning point of the curve y = x² + 8x + 3. (c) Solve x² + 8x + 3 = 0, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures. (6 marks)
steps: (b) Turning point is (−a, b) = (−4, −13) (B1). It is a minimum because the x² coefficient is positive.

worked.q: (a) Write 2x² − 12x + 5 in the form a(x + p)² + q. (b) Hence write down the minimum value of 2x² − 12x + 5 and the value of x at which it occurs. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Factor 2 from the first two terms only: 2(x² − 6x) + 5 (M1).
Complete the square inside: x² − 6x = (x − 3)² − 9, so 2[(x − 3)² − 9] + 5 (M1).
(b) (x − 3)² ≥ 0, smallest value 0 when x = 3, so the minimum value is −13 at x = 3 (B1). Check: 2(9) − 36 + 5 = −13. ✓

worked.q: A ball is thrown upwards. Its height h metres above the ground after t seconds is h = −5t² + 20t + 1. (a) Write h in the form a(t + p)² + q. (b) Write down the greatest height and when it occurs. (c) Find when the ball hits the ground, to 2 decimal places. (6 marks)
steps: (b) −5(t − 2)² ≤ 0 so h ≤ 21: greatest height 21 m when t = 2 seconds (B1).
t − 2 = ±√4.2 = ±2.049, so t = 4.05 or t = −0.05. Time cannot be negative, so reject t = −0.05 (A1). Check: −5(16.40) + 81 + 1 ≈ 0. ✓
